hops.afterHeading: One patient, two ways of remembering
hops.title: Where the letters sit on your keyboard
hops.text: Without looking, try to say where G, V and B sit on your keyboard. In a Vanderbilt University study, 100 typists averaged 72 words a minute at 94% accuracy, about six keystrokes a second. Handed a blank keyboard and 80 seconds, they placed an average of just 15 letters correctly. In a later experiment, 24 typists spent about two hours learning the unfamiliar Dvorak layout and then placed 16.5 of its letters on average, statistically no different from the 14.1 they placed on QWERTY after nearly 13 years of typing. Your fingers can find a key mid-word that you struggle to point to when asked.

sources.citation: Vanderbilt University Research News (Dec 4, 2013), reporting Snyder, Ashitaka, Shimada, Ulrich & Logan (2014), Attention, Perception, & Psychophysics 76(1):162-171.
Snyder KM, Ashitaka Y, Shimada H, Ulrich JE, Logan GD (2014). What skilled typists don't know about the QWERTY keyboard. Attention, Perception, & Psychophysics 76(1):162-171. PMID: 24101344.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A student with closed eyes holds both hands over a laptop with blank keys, beside an empty keyboard grid and a pencil.
image.caption: Typists averaged about six keystrokes a second, yet placed only about 15 letters correctly on a blank keyboard.

hops.afterHeading: The key experiment: lines that cross
hops.title: A haunted-house visit after amygdala damage
hops.text: For years patient S.M., whose amygdalae are both damaged, told researchers she hated snakes and spiders and tried to avoid them. Then the team took her to an exotic pet store. She held a live snake for over three minutes, touched its flicking tongue, asked 15 times to handle the larger snakes, and had to be stopped from touching a tarantula. She knew the larger snakes could bite; curiosity still drew her toward them. At the Waverly Hills Sanatorium haunted house she led five strangers down the dark hallways, rated her fear at zero, and startled one costumed monster by poking its head out of curiosity.

sources.citation: Feinstein JS, Adolphs R, Damasio A, Tranel D (2011). The human amygdala and the induction and experience of fear. Current Biology 21(1):34-38. PMCID: PMC3030206.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A calm visitor seen from behind taps a startled costumed monster on the head in a haunted-house hallway while others hang back.
image.caption: With both amygdalae damaged, S.M. said she hated snakes, yet reported very little fear while holding one.

hops.title: Stress shifts how people learn the weather-prediction task
hops.text: Lars Schwabe and Oliver Wolf had volunteers hold one hand in ice water near 0 °C for three minutes while being videotaped and watched by a cold, unresponsive experimenter; controls used warm water. Twenty-five minutes later both groups learned this lesson's weather-prediction task in a scanner, and both reached about 67% correct. They got there differently. Single-card rules best described 63% of controls but only 37% of stressed volunteers, and multi-card rules 10% against 35%. Stressed volunteers also recalled fewer details of the task. In controls, better performance went with more hippocampal activity; under stress, with more striatal and less hippocampal activity.

sources.citation: Schwabe L, Wolf OT (2012). Stress modulates the engagement of multiple memory systems in classification learning. Journal of Neuroscience 32(32):11042-11049. PMCID: PMC6621021.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A glass bowl of ice water sits beside patterned cue cards and small wooden sun and raindrop charms.
image.caption: After stress, volunteers predicted the weather about as well, but more of them relied on combinations of cards.

audio.title: Three stories about separate memory systems
audio.transcript:
Once you start looking for separate memory systems, they turn up in odd places: a video game at bedtime, a breath of carbon dioxide, and a soccer field.

First, bedtime Tetris. If you have ever played a block-dropping game for hours and then seen the shapes drifting behind your eyelids as you fall asleep, you know the feeling. In two thousand, the sleep researcher Robert Stickgold and his colleagues asked whether those sleep-onset images depend on declarative memory. They had people play Tetris, including five patients with amnesia and extensive damage to both medial temporal lobes. None of the five remembered playing from one session to the next. Yet three of them reported seeing shapes from the game as they drifted off to sleep, much as healthy players did. The shapes came back even when the memory of playing did not, and the researchers suggested that an implicit memory of the game supplied them.

Next, a twist on the lesson's rule that needed does not mean stored. You read that a patient with amygdala damage never acquired a conditioned sweat response, yet could still say which stimuli went together. Researchers at the University of Iowa have studied a rare patient known as S M, who has damage to both amygdalae. In twenty eleven they reported that she held a live snake for over three minutes, asked fifteen times to handle the bigger dangerous ones, and rated her fear at zero in a haunted house. You might conclude that her brain simply cannot produce fear. Two years later, a group including the same lead author tested that idea. They gave S M and two other patients with damage to both amygdalae a single breath of air containing thirty-five percent carbon dioxide. All three felt intense fear and had panic attacks, compared with only three of twelve healthy volunteers. While the healthy volunteers waited for the breath, their heart rate and sweating crept up. In the two patients whose heart rate could be measured, the rise was smaller, and the one patient with a usable sweat recording showed none. The authors suggested that the amygdala helps prepare us for threats we see or hear, while the suffocating feeling from carbon dioxide could set off fear and panic without it. Lose a structure, and you learn what it is needed for, not where every trace of fear lives.

Finally, what happens when an expert pays close attention to a movement that usually comes easily? In two thousand two, Sian Beilock and her colleagues tested experienced golfers and right-footed soccer players. Experienced golfers putted more accurately while doing a distracting second task than when told to attend to each step of their stroke. Experienced soccer players dribbled a slalom course better with their skilled right foot while distracted than while monitoring their foot. Switch them to their weaker left foot, though, or test beginners on either foot, and step-by-step attention helped instead. When a movement is well practised, watching closely how you make it can throw it off.
